idiom_name: cdylib + extern "C" symbol table via libloading (the only stable route)
alternative: Compose at compile time (Cargo features plus a trait-object registry chosen from configuration). If runtime pluggability is genuinely required, expose the component as a C-ABI cdylib loaded through a crate such as libloading, or run it out of process (subprocess/IPC or a WASM host) so replacement is a restart, not an unload.
implementation_notes: Rust has no stable ABI - the reference documents that type layout 'can be changed with each compilation' - so a component boundary can only be a C ABI surface: build the component as a cdylib exporting extern "C" factory/destroy symbols with repr(C) types, and load it with a third-party crate such as libloading, whose Library runs the library's termination routines on unload and documents that platform differences are not hidden. The idiomatic Rust answers to component configuration are compile-time (Cargo features plus a trait-object registry selected from configuration) or out-of-process (subprocess over IPC, or a WASM host such as wasmtime): in-process Rust-to-Rust dynamic linking is deliberately unsupported, and unloading code while references to it exist is undefined behaviour.
pitfalls: Never pass Rust types (String, Vec, trait objects, Result, enums with data) across the boundary: only repr(C) and scalar types are layout-stable, so richer values must be serialized or exchanged as an opaque pointer with an explicit destroy function.

Unloading is unsafe: any live reference into the library's code or data (trait-object vtables, Drop impls, callbacks, thread stacks) turns unload into a use-after-free, so the Library must outlive every symbol taken from it and unload may only follow a full drain - if at all.

Panics must not unwind across an extern "C" boundary (that is undefined behaviour): wrap exported functions in catch_unwind and return error codes, and expect host and component to be built with the same compiler since the Rust ABI is not a compatibility contract.
